Diamonds are forever

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we expose the illicit diamond trade and the greedy lengths syndicates will go to to get their hands on these precious stones.

Summary:
As with precious metals, diamonds are a profitable black market commodity. South African organized crime syndicates have infiltrated every sector of the diamond industry - from corrupting security staff at mines to falsifying Kimberley Process certificates in order to export illicit uncut stones. And while the police last year made one of the biggest illegal diamond industry busts to date, the syndicates are continuing plundering this lucrative resource. As with most illegal commodities, as long as there is a demand, there will be someone willing to supply.

Further information:
I have 3 unrelated sources willing to speak to me on camera. As two of them are involved in the industry, their id's will have to be hidden. Between the three of them they will cover every aspect of the illegal trade - from the zamas who mine the diamonds illegally, to the small time traders of illegal diamonds, to the bigger buyers and how most of these diamonds agin end up on the legal market. Zamas in Kimberley have agreed to speak to us on camera, and take us to where they operate. I have also been given several hidden camera clips of actual diamond deal sting operations, and a lot of still images of these same operations. I also have exclusive images of a lebanese man arrested at OR Tambo international airport in 2012, who was carrying 220 diamonds in his rectum. I have images of his arrest, x-rays of the diamonds inside of him as well as images of the diamonds recovered. I have been given documentary proof that this man, a Lebanese national, is affiliated to militant organisations such as Hamas and Hezbollah - who apparently buy diamonds in SA to use in barter agreements elsewhere on the African continent for goods such as weapons and ammunition. I am TRYING to verify the documents, but this is obviously difficult to do. There are various international reports confirming that diamonds are often used in terror finance and money laundering activities, although neither SARS or the FIC will confirm this on the record...

1 x R1200 petrol for source Big Blue who needs to drive down to Kimberley and cannot fly in.

Press Release:


Black Market Diamonds
Easy to transport and trade, diamonds could be the ultimate black market commodity. From bribing security staff at mines to falsifying process certificates to export illicit uncut stones, organised criminal syndicates have infiltrated every link in the process of getting a raw diamond out of the ground and into the precious stone trade, making handsome profits in the process. Carte Blanche investigates.



Script:


On Screen Text
In 1871 diamonds were discovered on Colesburg Kopje.
Within a month nearly 800 claims were cut into the hillock.
Historians described the resulting diamond rush as a stampede.

Voice
Between 1871 and 1914, some 50 000 miners sought their fortunes excavating what would become the world famous Kimberley Mine. As the miners toiled, a town was born. But with the extreme wealth came extreme greed, and more than a century later, nothing much has changed…

Link Devi
South Africa is the seventh largest diamond producing nation in the world, and while it’s a great source of revenue for our economy, we have become a soft target for diamond smugglers.

Voice
South Africa produces roughly 7 million carats of diamonds a year in the legal trade, ripe pickings for the black market.

Sound Up Source Big Blue
D: Are we talking big money?
A: We’re talking billions.
D: And how long has it been going on for?
A: As long as there’s been diamonds.

Voice
Our investigation into the illicit diamond trade took us to Kimberley in the Northern Cape – home to the “Big Hole”, but also a hotspot for black market diamonds. We arranged to meet three insiders who were willing to expose the inner workings of the illegal diamond trade at a secret location. Mr Blue describes himself as an intelligence officer.

Sound Up Source Big Blue
D: So what kind of work do you do?
A: Our main task is to gather intelligence on smuggling syndicates… on how they steal.

Voice
Mr Red was a licensed diamond trader who used his business as a front to make huge profits from illegal diamonds.

Sound Up Source Big Red
D: Why would somebody legally trading in diamonds want to trade illegally as well?
A: Because the profit margins are much higher… If you get an uncut diamond you just cut it and it’s legal. That’s the shortest way about it…

Voice
And Mr Yellow is a zama zama, or illegal miner, who spends his days searching for that one big score which will enable him to escape his life of crime and poverty.

Sound Up Source Big Yellow
D: Let’s say in a month, how many diamonds would you find?
A: Maybe, when you are lucky you can find once or twice a month. It depends, where did you dig.

Voice
In 2012 the Hawks, acting on a tip off, arrested a Lebanese man, Mohamad Ismail, pictured here, as he was about to leave the country.

Sound Up Big Blue
A: There was a suspect arrested at OR Tambo in 2012, with diamonds in his rectum, that was worth between 20 and 40 million rand.

Voice
Mr Blue believes Mohamad Ismail was a runner for a Lebanese smuggling syndicate with links to terrorist organisations.

Sound Up Mr Blue
A: We followed the leads and the tracks, and it led to a Palestinian group operating out of Beirut that’s got funding links with Al Qaeda and Hamas.
D: Why would terrorist organisations be interested in diamonds?
A: If you go buy firearms with 20 or 40 million, to supply ISIS or Al Qaeda or Hamas, it’s a whole truckload full of cash. You walk into those countries with 40 or 50 millions rands worth of diamonds – it’s a cupful. What’s the easiest to transport, a cupful of diamonds or a truckload of cash?

Voice
But to fully understand the scope of the illicit diamond trade in South Africa, we need to start at it’s roots.

Link Devi
On the face of it, it all looks normal, but behind me in this veldt, illegal diamond mining is going on right now.

Voice
This is one of many sites on the outskirts of Kimberley where zama zamas ply their trade. The heaps of diamond rich soil visible in this hidden camera footage are referred
to as feature, and it’s what the zamas are after.

Sound Up Big Blue
D:Tell me about the zama zamas?
A: Massive problem.
D: You say massive, how big?
A: Very big, that’s what fuels the diamond industry in and around Kimberley.

Sound Up Mr Yellow
D: Have you found diamonds?
A: Yes.
D: Big ones, small ones?
A: The one, it was 2.45 carat. And the small one.
D: 2.45 carats is quite big?
A: No it’s not really big.
D: You mean people find even bigger ones?
A: Ja, even 17 carats.

Voice
Unlike illegal gold mining, diamond zamas usually don’t have to brave days underground in abandoned mine shafts. These zamas dig up surface level soil, often in areas adjacent to large diamond mines, and put the soil through a simple sieving process.

Sound Up Mr Yellow
you’ve got a lot of feature. So you going to take that “feature” and “rof” it… So after “roffing” we sieve, after sieving we sort.

Voice
The “feature” is roughed through a rudimentary sieve. If these zamas had found a big enough diamond it would be visible here. But just in case they miss one, the roughed material is put through a secondary sorting process.

Sound Up Mr Yellow
D: On average, in a good month, how much will you make?
A: I can make maybe R20 000
D: And on a bad month? Zero?
A: On a bad month, nothing.

Voice
And when the pickings are poor, the more organised zamas resort to outright theft at the mines themselves.

Sound Up Mr Blue
They get access with the help of security personnel into the mines, from where they steal. They dig in the mines, get warned if there is any impending operation, and that’s where they get the good diamonds from.

Sound Up Mr Yellow
D: How much do you pay the security guards?
A: R200
D: Per night?
A: Ja
D: That’s it?
A: Ja.

Voice
According to Brigadier Hangwani Mulaudzi, spokesperson for the Hawks, corruption in the diamond trade is an ongoing problem.

Sound Up Brig Mulaudzi
There are instances as well, that we know, that there are some members that are within the South African Police Service, that are involved in this diamond trade, the illegal diamond trade.

Voice
Illegal mining and theft are not the only sources of illicit diamonds – a lot of the precious gems are smuggled into SA from neigbouring countries like Botswana, Zimbabwe and Namibia.

Sound Up Big Blue
D: So these diamonds that come here from the rest of Africa need to be cut and polished into the form that we understand diamonds?
A: Yes. It’s because we’ve got an easy market to swing these things, there’s a high demand in SA for the stuff.

Link Devi
The zama zamas and mine employees are at the bottom of the food chain, despite the risk they don’t get the big bucks. But go up that chain, to the buyers, and you hit jackpot.

Voice:
Unless you’re a licensed diamond trader, you can’t legally be in possesion of uncut diamonds. But once those diamonds are cut and polished, they can be legitimised with false paper work. Your treasured wedding ring could contain an illegal diamond and you’d never know it.

Sound Up Mr Red
D: So you’d buy it illegally for 20 000…
A: Yes, cut it, it doesn’t cost you much, and there you’ve got a R100 000 diamond.
D: Just like that?
A: Just like that.

Voice
This footage shows an undercover agent negotiating an uncut diamond deal in a hotel room in the Free State.

Sound Up Footage
UC Operative: Jeez, that’s small. You know I can almost not do anything with this? But I’ll buy it just so that we can open the channel. Let see. Look carefully now, you see it’s at zero? You see it’s carat?

Voice
After inspecting the merchandise, the agent wheighs the stones on a digital scale similar to these.

Sound Up Footage
UC Operative: Everything together is 3.5 carat. That one doesn’t mean much, that one is milky. How much do you want for this?

Voice
Eventually the agent agrees to pay the seller R5000 for the relatively poor quality stones. If this was a real deal, the buyer would probably have been able to resell the gems for about R25 000.

Sound Up Big Red
They would call you, and say they’ve got a three carater or a two carater diamond they want to sell. Where do we meet, you can meet them anywhere, you can meet at the Wimpy, the Spur or whatever you know. It doesn’t matter.

Voice
This footage shows another illegal deal on a construction site. The uncut diamond visible here weighs roughly four carats and you can buy it on the black market for about R60 000. Once you’ve had it cut and polished, it would sell for between R150 000 and R200 000 on the legitimate market.




Link Devi
Eventually our diamonds are smuggled out of the country, and end up in the hands of foreign byuers, in Dubai, India, Hong Kong and Belgium.

Sound Up Brig Mulaudzi
we are talking about billions of rands that has been smuggled out of this country.

Voice
Mohamad Ismail plead guilty to the illegal possesion and sale of unpolished diamonds, but he didn’t see any jailtime. Instead he was fined R250 000.

Sound Up Mr Blue
How many times was this guy in and out the country? One deal, between 20 and 40 million, he was in and out of the country 20 times. Just one runner.

Sound Up Brig Mulaudzi
but I think that is something that we still continue to grapple with with the NPA to see if can’t we do something with these fines you know, maybe people must start to sit in jail, feel the pain for what they’ve done

Voice
We asked the Hawks if they were aware that South African diamonds might be funding international terrorism.

Sound Up Brig. Mulaudzi
that rumor we cannot rule it out but so far, we do not have anything concrete to suggest that these diamonds are being used for any terrorist activities.

Voice
And with the high profits involved, sophisticated smuggling networks and an insatiable international demand, this is not a problem that is going to go away any time soon.

Sound Up Brig Mulaudzi
And we are working very hard to make sure that these people who are responsible for these things, that we arrest them.

Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 08 May 2015 Press Release: Black Market Diamonds Easy to transport and trade, diamonds could be the ultimate black market commodity. From bribing security staff at mines to falsifying process certificates to export illicit uncut stones, organised criminal syndicates have infiltrated every link in the process of getting a raw diamond out of the ground and into the precious stone trade, making handsome profits in the process. Carte Blanche investigates. Script: On Screen Text In 1871 diamonds were discovered on Colesburg Kopje. Within a month nearly 800 claims were cut into the hillock. Historians described the resulting diamond rush as a stampede. Voice Between 1871 and 1914, some 50 000 miners sought their fortunes excavating what would become the world famous Kimberley Mine. As the miners toiled, a town was born. But with the extreme wealth came extreme greed, and more than a century later, nothing much has changed… Link Devi South Africa is the seventh largest diamond producing nation in the world, and while it’s a great source of revenue for our economy, we have become a soft target for diamond smugglers. Voice South Africa produces roughly 7 million carats of diamonds a year in the legal trade, ripe pickings for the black market. Sound Up Source Big Blue D: Are we talking big money? A: We’re talking billions. D: And how long has it been going on for? A: As long as there’s been diamonds. Voice Our investigation into the illicit diamond trade took us to Kimberley in the Northern Cape – home to the “Big Hole”, but also a hotspot for black market diamonds. We arranged to meet three insiders who were willing to expose the inner workings of the illegal diamond trade at a secret location. Mr Blue describes himself as an intelligence officer. Sound Up Source Big Blue D: So what kind of work do you do? A: Our main task is to gather intelligence on smuggling syndicates… on how they steal. Voice Mr Red was a licensed diamond trader who used his business as a front to make huge profits from illegal diamonds. Sound Up Source Big Red D: Why would somebody legally trading in diamonds want to trade illegally as well? A: Because the profit margins are much higher… If you get an uncut diamond you just cut it and it’s legal. That’s the shortest way about it… Voice And Mr Yellow is a zama zama, or illegal miner, who spends his days searching for that one big score which will enable him to escape his life of crime and poverty. Sound Up Source Big Yellow D: Let’s say in a month, how many diamonds would you find? A: Maybe, when you are lucky you can find once or twice a month. It depends, where did you dig. Voice In 2012 the Hawks, acting on a tip off, arrested a Lebanese man, Mohamad Ismail, pictured here, as he was about to leave the country. Sound Up Big Blue A: There was a suspect arrested at OR Tambo in 2012, with diamonds in his rectum, that was worth between 20 and 40 million rand. Voice Mr Blue believes Mohamad Ismail was a runner for a Lebanese smuggling syndicate with links to terrorist organisations. Sound Up Mr Blue A: We followed the leads and the tracks, and it led to a Palestinian group operating out of Beirut that’s got funding links with Al Qaeda and Hamas. D: Why would terrorist organisations be interested in diamonds? A: If you go buy firearms with 20 or 40 million, to supply ISIS or Al Qaeda or Hamas, it’s a whole truckload full of cash. You walk into those countries with 40 or 50 millions rands worth of diamonds – it’s a cupful. What’s the easiest to transport, a cupful of diamonds or a truckload of cash? Voice But to fully understand the scope of the illicit diamond trade in South Africa, we need to start at it’s roots. Link Devi On the face of it, it all looks normal, but behind me in this veldt, illegal diamond mining is going on right now. Voice This is one of many sites on the outskirts of Kimberley where zama zamas ply their trade. The heaps of diamond rich soil visible in this hidden camera footage are referred to as feature, and it’s what the zamas are after. Sound Up Big Blue D:Tell me about the zama zamas? A: Massive problem. D: You say massive, how big? A: Very big, that’s what fuels the diamond industry in and around Kimberley. Sound Up Mr Yellow D: Have you found diamonds? A: Yes. D: Big ones, small ones? A: The one, it was 2.45 carat. And the small one. D: 2.45 carats is quite big? A: No it’s not really big. D: You mean people find even bigger ones? A: Ja, even 17 carats. Voice Unlike illegal gold mining, diamond zamas usually don’t have to brave days underground in abandoned mine shafts. These zamas dig up surface level soil, often in areas adjacent to large diamond mines, and put the soil through a simple sieving process. Sound Up Mr Yellow you’ve got a lot of feature. So you going to take that “feature” and “rof” it… So after “roffing” we sieve, after sieving we sort. Voice The “feature” is roughed through a rudimentary sieve. If these zamas had found a big enough diamond it would be visible here. But just in case they miss one, the roughed material is put through a secondary sorting process. Sound Up Mr Yellow D: On average, in a good month, how much will you make? A: I can make maybe R20 000 D: And on a bad month? Zero? A: On a bad month, nothing. Voice And when the pickings are poor, the more organised zamas resort to outright theft at the mines themselves. Sound Up Mr Blue They get access with the help of security personnel into the mines, from where they steal. They dig in the mines, get warned if there is any impending operation, and that’s where they get the good diamonds from. Sound Up Mr Yellow D: How much do you pay the security guards? A: R200 D: Per night? A: Ja D: That’s it? A: Ja. Voice According to Brigadier Hangwani Mulaudzi, spokesperson for the Hawks, corruption in the diamond trade is an ongoing problem. Sound Up Brig Mulaudzi There are instances as well, that we know, that there are some members that are within the South African Police Service, that are involved in this diamond trade, the illegal diamond trade. Voice Illegal mining and theft are not the only sources of illicit diamonds – a lot of the precious gems are smuggled into SA from neigbouring countries like Botswana, Zimbabwe and Namibia. Sound Up Big Blue D: So these diamonds that come here from the rest of Africa need to be cut and polished into the form that we understand diamonds? A: Yes. It’s because we’ve got an easy market to swing these things, there’s a high demand in SA for the stuff. Link Devi The zama zamas and mine employees are at the bottom of the food chain, despite the risk they don’t get the big bucks. But go up that chain, to the buyers, and you hit jackpot. Voice: Unless you’re a licensed diamond trader, you can’t legally be in possesion of uncut diamonds. But once those diamonds are cut and polished, they can be legitimised with false paper work. Your treasured wedding ring could contain an illegal diamond and you’d never know it. Sound Up Mr Red D: So you’d buy it illegally for 20 000… A: Yes, cut it, it doesn’t cost you much, and there you’ve got a R100 000 diamond. D: Just like that? A: Just like that. Voice This footage shows an undercover agent negotiating an uncut diamond deal in a hotel room in the Free State. Sound Up Footage UC Operative: Jeez, that’s small. You know I can almost not do anything with this? But I’ll buy it just so that we can open the channel. Let see. Look carefully now, you see it’s at zero? You see it’s carat? Voice After inspecting the merchandise, the agent wheighs the stones on a digital scale similar to these. Sound Up Footage UC Operative: Everything together is 3.5 carat. That one doesn’t mean much, that one is milky. How much do you want for this? Voice Eventually the agent agrees to pay the seller R5000 for the relatively poor quality stones. If this was a real deal, the buyer would probably have been able to resell the gems for about R25 000. Sound Up Big Red They would call you, and say they’ve got a three carater or a two carater diamond they want to sell. Where do we meet, you can meet them anywhere, you can meet at the Wimpy, the Spur or whatever you know. It doesn’t matter. Voice This footage shows another illegal deal on a construction site. The uncut diamond visible here weighs roughly four carats and you can buy it on the black market for about R60 000. Once you’ve had it cut and polished, it would sell for between R150 000 and R200 000 on the legitimate market. Link Devi Eventually our diamonds are smuggled out of the country, and end up in the hands of foreign byuers, in Dubai, India, Hong Kong and Belgium. Sound Up Brig Mulaudzi we are talking about billions of rands that has been smuggled out of this country. Voice Mohamad Ismail plead guilty to the illegal possesion and sale of unpolished diamonds, but he didn’t see any jailtime. Instead he was fined R250 000. Sound Up Mr Blue How many times was this guy in and out the country? One deal, between 20 and 40 million, he was in and out of the country 20 times. Just one runner. Sound Up Brig Mulaudzi but I think that is something that we still continue to grapple with with the NPA to see if can’t we do something with these fines you know, maybe people must start to sit in jail, feel the pain for what they’ve done Voice We asked the Hawks if they were aware that South African diamonds might be funding international terrorism. Sound Up Brig. Mulaudzi that rumor we cannot rule it out but so far, we do not have anything concrete to suggest that these diamonds are being used for any terrorist activities. Voice And with the high profits involved, sophisticated smuggling networks and an insatiable international demand, this is not a problem that is going to go away any time soon. Sound Up Brig Mulaudzi And we are working very hard to make sure that these people who are responsible for these things, that we arrest them. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): we expose the illicit diamond trade and the greedy lengths syndicates will go to to get their hands on these precious stones.
metadata.Summary: As with precious metals, diamonds are a profitable black market commodity. South African organized crime syndicates have infiltrated every sector of the diamond industry - from corrupting security staff at mines to falsifying Kimberley Process certificates in order to export illicit uncut stones. And while the police last year made one of the biggest illegal diamond industry busts to date, the syndicates are continuing plundering this lucrative resource. As with most illegal commodities, as long as there is a demand, there will be someone willing to supply.
metadata.Further information: I have 3 unrelated sources willing to speak to me on camera. As two of them are involved in the industry, their id's will have to be hidden. Between the three of them they will cover every aspect of the illegal trade - from the zamas who mine the diamonds illegally, to the small time traders of illegal diamonds, to the bigger buyers and how most of these diamonds agin end up on the legal market. Zamas in Kimberley have agreed to speak to us on camera, and take us to where they operate. I have also been given several hidden camera clips of actual diamond deal sting operations, and a lot of still images of these same operations. I also have exclusive images of a lebanese man arrested at OR Tambo international airport in 2012, who was carrying 220 diamonds in his rectum. I have images of his arrest, x-rays of the diamonds inside of him as well as images of the diamonds recovered. I have been given documentary proof that this man, a Lebanese national, is affiliated to militant organisations such as Hamas and Hezbollah - who apparently buy diamonds in SA to use in barter agreements elsewhere on the African continent for goods such as weapons and ammunition. I am TRYING to verify the documents, but this is obviously difficult to do. There are various international reports confirming that diamonds are often used in terror finance and money laundering activities, although neither SARS or the FIC will confirm this on the record...
